title: Games That Travel
bigQuestion: How did ball games move from one town to towns across the world?

story.title: A Ball With No Writing
story.kicker: An old ball rolls out of a gym closet, and a class wonders where games come from.
paragraphs: Mr. Reyes opens the gym closet. An old ball rolls out. It has no name on it. The leather is smooth and dark from many hands.
"Who made this game?" asks Nia. Mr. Reyes smiles. "Soccer rules were first written down in London in 1863," he says. "But people kicked balls long before that."
He points to a map on the wall. "Ships carried balls across oceans. Teachers carried rules to new schools. That is how a game moves."
Nia holds the ball up to the light. She thinks of all the towns it might have visited. Then she sets it back on the shelf.
story.think: What does a game need to move to a new town: a ball, a rule, or both?

lessons.title: Rubber Balls in Old Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: People in old Mexico played with rubber balls on stone courts over 3,000 years ago.
reading: People in Mexico and Central America played a ball game over 3,000 years ago. Their balls were made of *rubber*. Rubber comes from the milky sap of a tree.
Players used a long, narrow *ball court* with walls on each side. A huge stone court still stands at Chichén Itzá in Mexico. Two stone rings sit high on its walls.
Spanish visitors saw the game in the 1500s. Europe had no rubber balls then. The bouncing balls amazed the visitors.

words.d: a bouncy stuff made from the sap of certain trees
a long stone alley with walls where the old Mexican ball game was played

lessons.title: Kick Ball in Old China
lessons.mainIdea: In old China, people played a kicking game called cuju more than 2,000 years ago.
reading: People in old China played a game called *cuju*. The name means "kick ball." It was played more than 2,000 years ago.
Soldiers played cuju to stay strong. Later, people at the emperor's palace played it too. The ball was made of leather.
China kept written records about cuju. FIFA is the world soccer group. It has called cuju the oldest kicking game with written history.

words.d: an old Chinese kicking game; the name means "kick ball"

lessons.title: The Creator's Game
lessons.mainIdea: Native nations of North America played lacrosse long before Europeans came.
reading: Native nations of North America played a stick-and-ball game for hundreds of years. The Haudenosaunee, also called the Iroquois, are one of those nations.
French visitors saw the game in the 1600s. They gave it a French name, *lacrosse*. Many Haudenosaunee people call it the Creator's Game.
The Haudenosaunee still play today. They have their own national team. It plays against other countries in world contests.

words.d: a stick-and-ball game first played by Native nations of North America
a group of Native nations, also called the Iroquois

lessons.title: Rules Written in London
lessons.mainIdea: On 26 October 1863, clubs in London formed the Football Association to share one set of rules.
reading: Long ago, English schools each played football their own way. Some let players carry the ball. Others only let them kick it.
On 26 October 1863, club leaders met at a tavern in London. They formed the *Football Association*. They wrote one set of rules to share.
People shortened "association" to *soccer*. That is where the word comes from. In England, the game is still called football.

words.d: the group formed in London in 1863 to write shared football rules
a short name made from the word association

lessons.title: Two Balls in a Suitcase
lessons.mainIdea: People who learned soccer in England carried the game to South America.
reading: British people living in Argentina started a soccer club in Buenos Aires in 1867. It was one of the first in South America.
Charles Miller was born in Brazil. He went to school in England and learned soccer there. In 1894 he came home with two balls and a rule book.
Soccer grew fast in South America. In 1930, Uruguay held the first World Cup. Uruguay won it, too.

words.d: the world soccer contest between countries, first held in Uruguay in 1930

lessons.title: Countries Join Hands
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904 so soccer groups from different countries could work together.
reading: By 1904, many countries had soccer groups. On 21 May 1904, seven of them met in Paris. They formed *FIFA*.
FIFA runs contests between countries, like the World Cup. Another group, the IFAB, keeps the Laws of the Game. The IFAB began in 1886.
FIFA started with seven members. Today it has 211 member associations from around the world.

words.d: the world soccer group, founded in Paris in 1904
the group that keeps soccer's Laws of the Game, begun in 1886

sections.title: Hoops and Bats on the Move

lessons.title: Peach Baskets in Springfield
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith made basketball in a YMCA gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in December 1891.
reading: James Naismith was a teacher from Canada. He worked at a *YMCA* school in Springfield, Massachusetts. In December 1891 he made up an indoor game for winter.
He nailed two peach baskets up high. He wrote 13 rules. His class had 18 students, so nine played on each side.
His rules were printed in the school paper in January 1892. YMCA teachers took the game to other gyms. It spread to many countries.

words.d: the Young Men's Christian Association, which ran the school where Naismith taught

lessons.title: Baseball Sails to Japan
lessons.mainIdea: An American teacher brought baseball to Japan in 1872, and a Chicago team toured the world in 1888.
reading: Horace Wilson was an American teacher in Tokyo, Japan. In 1872 he taught his students to play baseball. Japan later put him in its Baseball Hall of Fame.
In 1888, Albert Spalding led a *tour* with Chicago baseball players. They sailed around the world. They played games in Australia and Egypt.
Today baseball is a favorite game in Japan. High school teams there play in a big national contest every summer.

words.d: a long trip to many places, stopping to play or show something
